title: Hal Blaine - Wikipedia
notes: Harold Simon Belsky, 5 February 1929 (Holyoke, Massachusetts) - 11 March 2019 (Palm Desert, California). To Hartford at seven; drums from eight, his first kit at 13; survived the Hartford circus fire, 6 July 1944; to California in 1944. Lessons with Roy Knapp, who had taught Gene Krupa, 1949-52; strip clubs in Chicago, where he learned to sight-read; Count Basie's band, Patti Page and Tommy Sands; then sessions. A core member of the Wrecking Crew, which he named. Be My Baby (1963) at Gold Star: 'The pattern was created when Blaine accidentally hit the snare on just the fourth beat, instead of the two and four.' Claimed over 35,000 sessions and 6,000 singles; 150 US top ten hits, 40 number ones. The 'Hal Blaine Strikes Again' rubber stamp. Credited with popularising the 'pshh-shup' hat opened and closed on Johnny Rivers's Poor Side of Town. Six consecutive Grammy Records of the Year (A Taste of Honey, Strangers in the Night, Up, Up and Away, Mrs. Robinson, Aquarius/Let the Sunshine In, Bridge over Troubled Water). Rock and Roll Hall of Fame 2000 (with Earl Palmer), Modern Drummer Hall of Fame 2010, Grammy Lifetime Achievement 2018. Family statement: 'May he rest forever on 2 and 4'.

title: Richard Williams, 'Hal Blaine obituary', The Guardian, 12 March 2019
notes: 'He knew when to keep it simple in order to make a song distinctive when played on the radio.' Be My Baby's intro 'a brusque bom bom-bom BANG!'; 'his driving beat and epic tom-tom fills formed the foundation of Phil Spector's Wall of Sound'. Pet Sounds: 'a box of exotic percussion devices', soft-drink bottles for Caroline, No. Kept kits set up to his specification in several studios (Gold Star, Sunset Sound, RCA, Western). Lessons with Roy Knapp after the family moved to southern California; 'always credited his fellow drummer Earl Palmer with giving him a leg up ... Palmer soon had more sessions than he could handle, and began passing some of them on to Blaine.' Named the Wrecking Crew after the 'blue-blazer guys'. Often brought in to replace a group's drummer in the studio; only the Byrds' Michael Clarke resented it; Micky Dolenz and Dennis Wilson imitated his parts on TV and on tour. 'A gregarious man who mentored younger drummers.' Palmer: 'Hal never had good jazz chops, but that don't make him not a hell of a drummer for what he did.' Max Weinberg on Be My Baby. His beat on California Dreamin', Mr Tambourine Man, Good Vibrations, Then He Kissed Me, MacArthur Park, Eve of Destruction, I Got You Babe, These Boots Are Made for Walkin'.

title: Hal Blaine, Rock & Roll Hall of Fame (inducted 2000, Award for Musical Excellence, by Mike Stoller)
notes: 'The most recorded drummer in history ... the accompanist to Phil Spector's Wall of Sound'; forty number one singles. Max Weinberg's essay: 'If Hal Blaine had played drums only on the Ronettes' Be My Baby, his name would still be forever uttered with reverence and respect for the power of his big beat.' Stoller: 'the steamroller behind the wall of sound'.

title: The Beach Boys, 'Good Vibrations' studio film, 1966 (as edited from the documentary Doin' It Again), YouTube uVlSVkzbJDA
notes: Black and white. The drummer at the kit with Carl Wilson, from 1:20 to 2:35: dark hair combed back, clean-shaven, a pale short-sleeved shirt open at the neck, a wristwatch, light trousers. The uploader says the film is 'more or less lip synced and acted for the purposes of promotion'. Identified here as Blaine because he drummed the Good Vibrations sessions (the Songsterr tab's track names him, with Jim Gordon); no caption in the clip names him.

title: 'Hal Blaine's Monster Set', Donn's Drum Vault, YouTube N0KwNDEwm1Y
notes: Donn Bennett demonstrates the set he says Blaine 'played on literally thousands of the most significant pop recordings': a long row of yellow fibreglass concert toms over Ludwig drums in a blue sparkle, a road case stencilled 'HAL BLAINE ... SNARE SET 1'.

title: Be My Baby - Wikipedia
notes: The Ronettes; produced by Phil Spector at Gold Star on 29 July 1963, arranged by Jack Nitzsche, engineered by Larry Levine; released August 1963, US number 2. 'The recording opens with two bars of a drum beat with prominent reverb; the snare drum, striking on the fourth beat of each bar until the chorus.' Blaine: 'That famous drum intro was an accident. I was supposed to play the snare on the second beat as well as the fourth, but I dropped a stick ... it became: Bum-ba-bum-BOOM!' Rehearsed four hours; Michael Spencer: 'the pause towards the end of the song where the drums go boom-ba-boom-boom'. Many later songs replicate the drum phrase.

title: Mr. Tambourine Man - Wikipedia
notes: The Byrds' version: recorded at Columbia, Hollywood, 20 January 1965, produced by Terry Melcher, who hired the Wrecking Crew; McGuinn the only Byrd playing. Released 12 April 1965, US and UK number one. Hal Blaine on drums, Larry Knechtel bass, Jerry Cole and Bill Pitman guitars.

title: Help Me, Rhonda - Wikipedia
notes: The Today! version (January 1965) 'more of a laid-back shuffle'; re-recorded with a punchier arrangement and released as a single in April 1965, US number one, on Summer Days (And Summer Nights!!). Personnel per Craig Slowinski: Hal Blaine on drums and timbales. Wilson: 'I would've made a better rhythm - it wasn't in the pocket.'

title: California Girls - Wikipedia
notes: Backing track at Western, Hollywood, 6 April 1965, 44 takes; on Summer Days (And Summer Nights!!), 5 July 1965, single 12 July, US number 3. Personnel per Craig Slowinski: Hal Blaine on drums, Billy Strange on tambourine.

title: Eve of Destruction (song) - Wikipedia
notes: Barry McGuire, recorded 12-15 July 1965, Dunhill; P. F. Sloan on guitar and harmonica with Wrecking Crew musicians, Hal Blaine on drums. A US number one.

title: California Dreamin' - Wikipedia
notes: The Mamas & the Papas, single December 1965, US number 4 in March 1966; produced by Lou Adler. Hal Blaine on drums and tambourine.

title: Wouldn't It Be Nice - Wikipedia
notes: Instrumental tracking at Gold Star, 22 January 1966, 21 takes, live with no overdubs; 'The exception was drummer Hal Blaine, who wore headphones and was tasked with signaling the other musicians to play on cue', the 12-string being played in the control room. Pet Sounds, 16 May 1966; the single US number 8. Hal Blaine on drums.

title: The Boxer - Wikipedia
notes: Simon & Garfunkel; single 21 March 1969. 'The song has only one drumbeat, played during the lie-la-lie refrain'; Roy Halee set Blaine's drums in front of an elevator in the Columbia offices. Blaine: 'Roy had me come down on my snare drum as hard as I could. In that hallway, by the elevator shaft, it sounded like a cannon shot!'

title: Strangers in the Night - Wikipedia
notes: Sinatra at United Western, 11 April 1966, with Ernie Freeman's arrangement: 'Hal Blaine was the drummer at the recording; according to Blaine, he reused the drum beat from Be My Baby by the Ronettes in a slower and softer arrangement.'

title: Jim Gordon (musician) - Wikipedia
notes: 'The protege of studio drummer Hal Blaine, Gordon performed on many notable recordings in the 1960s, including Pet Sounds.'

title: Karen Carpenter - Wikipedia
notes: 'According to the session drummer Hal Blaine, Karen played on many of the Carpenters' album cuts and he played on most of the studio sessions when she did not play drums'; she approved, 'easier to record Carpenter's guide vocal without its spilling onto the drum mics'. Blaine praised her drumming.

title: Max Weinberg - Wikipedia
notes: His influences listed as D. J. Fontana, Charlie Watts, Dino Danelli, Hal Blaine and others.
